title: Garden and Ember
premise: August Dunmore steals memories for a living, bottling other people's pasts into charms she sells in Grayhollow, a city where magic is outlawed and memory-thieves are burned. When a dying courier presses a map of the Ember Road into her hands, August learns the old covenant binding the human realm to the garden-realm of Virelle was broken twelve years ago — the same night her own childhood memories were taken. The map leads to three scattered keystones, each guarded by someone who remembers what August cannot. As she gathers them, she discovers she herself is the fourth keystone: the covenant's living seal, and restoring it will erase everything she has become. In the end, August refuses both erasure and abandonment, forging a new covenant that demands not one person's sacrifice but the city's honest remembering — and pays for it with the only thing she has left to give: her name.
about_author: Ivo Crane is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing confiscated letters in a coastal city and now writes fantasy about people who keep things they shouldn't. Garden and Ember is their third novel.

chapters.title: The Weight of Borrowed Years
chapters.summary: August works the night market, selling bottled memories to grieving buyers, POV hers. A routine sale goes wrong when a customer recognizes a charm's contents as his own stolen past, forcing August to flee through Grayhollow's ash-lit alleys. The beat establishes her cynicism and the city's fear of magic, ending on her quiet dread that some of the memories she sells might be her own.

chapters.title: A Stranger at the Door
chapters.summary: Still August's POV. A bleeding stranger collapses into her workshop, pressing a wax-sealed map into her hands and whispering 'the garden remembers' before dying. City wardens arrive hunting him; August hides the map and lies for the first time to authority. The emotional beat is terror mixed with a strange recognition — the stranger's face feels familiar in a way she can't explain.

chapters.title: What the Wardens Burn
chapters.summary: August investigates the stranger's identity while dodging warden patrols, POV hers. She finds his lodging ransacked and a charred photograph showing a woman with her own face, younger. Her fence, Odile, warns her to burn the map. The beat deepens the mystery of August's missing twelve years and hardens her resolve: whoever she was, someone killed to bury it.

chapters.title: The First Keystone: Salt
chapters.summary: Following the map's first thread to a drowned chapel on the coast, August meets Brannoc, a disgraced warden who guards the salt keystone out of guilt, POV shared between them. He recognizes her name from an execution list dated twelve years ago — her own. The beat is reluctant alliance; Brannoc agrees to guide her because he owes the dead stranger his life.

chapters.title: Memories Not Mine
chapters.summary: Brannoc teaches August how keystones resonate with covenant-bearers, and when she touches the salt stone, she experiences a flash: a garden, a woman singing, fire. POV hers, disoriented secondhand memory. She realizes her stolen childhood lives inside the covenant itself. The emotional beat is grief for a self she can't access, sharpening her hunger to reach the next keystone.

chapters.title: The Ember Road
chapters.summary: Traveling the old magic road toward the second keystone, August and Brannoc are ambushed by Hollow Men — enforcers of the Ash Court, which replaced the covenant with control. POV alternates. They escape when August instinctively works magic she shouldn't know. The beat is rising danger and August's growing suspicion that her body remembers what her mind lost.

chapters.title: The Woman Who Sings to Roots
chapters.summary: In a border village, they find Sefa, the singer from August's flash-vision, now old and tending a hidden garden, POV Sefa's. Sefa reveals August was the covenant's child-ward, raised in Virelle until the Breaking Night. She offers truth but warns the third keystone's guardian hates August's kind. The beat is warmth and revelation, the first place August feels she belongs.

chapters.title: The Second Keystone: Bone
chapters.summary: Sefa surrenders the bone keystone she has guarded for twelve years, POV August's. Holding it, August recovers a full memory: the Breaking Night, the Ash Court's founder — her former mentor, Wren Halloway — shattering the covenant to hoard its power. The beat is fury crystallizing into purpose; August stops running and starts hunting.

chapters.title: Ash Court
chapters.summary: POV Wren Halloway, antagonist chapter. Wren senses the keystones moving and dispatches the Hollow Men, revealing her philosophy: the covenant was slavery dressed as harmony, and she freed humanity by burning it. The beat complicates the moral landscape — Wren believes she saved the city, and readers should half-believe her too.

chapters.title: The Price of the Charm-Seller
chapters.summary: Captured by wardens, August bargains her way free by selling Wren's location, betraying Brannoc's trust, POV hers. Odile bails her out but reveals she sold information about August weeks ago. The beat is betrayal layered on betrayal, forcing August to confront that survival in Grayhollow has made her exactly the kind of person who trades people.

chapters.title: Reckoning at the Drowned Chapel
chapters.summary: August returns to apologize to Brannoc and finds the chapel sacked, Brannoc dying, POV hers then his. With his last breath he forgives her and gives her the salt keystone, calling her 'seal-bearer.' The beat is devastating guilt transformed into responsibility — she can no longer claim she's only surviving; others die for her path.

chapters.title: The Third Guardian
chapters.summary: August seeks the final keystone's guardian: Tam Vess, the man whose stolen memory she sold in chapter one, POV alternating. He has spent twelve years hollowed by its loss and hates memory-thieves above all. The beat is a standoff where August must offer the one currency she has — she lets him take a memory from her, choosing which, and it costs her more than expected.

chapters.title: What August Gave Away
chapters.summary: Tam takes the memory of Sefa's village, leaving August unable to feel the belonging she'd found there, POV hers. She keeps the ember keystone he relinquishes but understands now the covenant's true demand: it runs on given memory, freely surrendered. The beat is loss with clarity — she finally grasps what restoration will require of her personally.

chapters.title: The Garden That Waits
chapters.summary: With three keystones, August crosses into Virelle through the Ember Road's last gate, POV hers. The garden-realm is dying, gray at the edges, sustained only by the memory she carries unknowingly. She meets the covenant's remnant spirit, which shows her the fourth keystone: herself. The beat is awe curdling into horror as she learns restoration means her unmaking.

chapters.title: Seal-Bearer
chapters.summary: The spirit explains the original covenant: a living seal who holds the boundary between realms, giving memory continuously so both worlds remember each other. August was born to it; Wren stole her memories to break the seal. POV hers. The beat is the book's central choice laid bare — restore the old covenant and dissolve into function, or let both realms slowly forget and fade.

chapters.title: Wren's Argument
chapters.summary: Wren confronts August in Virelle, offering alliance instead of war: destroy the keystones entirely, free both realms from the covenant's hunger forever, POV Wren's. She reveals the covenant consumed the previous seal — August's mother. The beat is genuine temptation; Wren isn't lying, and August must weigh her mother's fate against two worlds' survival.

chapters.title: The Breaking Night, Whole
chapters.summary: August recovers her final stolen memory from within the ember keystone: the complete Breaking Night, including her own choice as a child to hide the seal rather than be used, POV hers. She realizes Wren didn't just steal — August resisted first. The beat reclaims her agency across time; she has always been the one who decides what the covenant becomes.

chapters.title: Reforging
chapters.summary: Climax begins: August returns to Grayhollow with the keystones and publicly works magic in the market square, forcing the city to see what outlawing memory cost them, POV multiple citizens briefly then hers. Wren attacks with the Hollow Men. The beat is open defiance — August refuses secrecy, betting that a covenant needs witnesses, not just a seal.

chapters.title: Ember and Ash
chapters.summary: Battle in the square as August begins the reforging, keystones resonating, memories flooding every citizen with the forgotten past, POV shifting rapidly among townsfolk experiencing returned memories. Wren falters when her own buried grief returns. The beat is chaos becoming communion — the city remembers together, and collective memory weakens Wren more than any weapon.

chapters.title: The New Covenant
chapters.summary: August rejects both options — dissolution or destruction — and forges a third path: a covenant renewed by the city's freely given memories, each citizen contributing willingly, with her as witness rather than seal, POV hers. Wren, undone by remembered love, stands down. The beat is triumph earned through refusal of easy sacrifice; the magic stabilizes because thousands carry it now.

chapters.title: A Name Given Back
chapters.summary: Resolution: the price surfaces — the covenant took August's name as its fee, and no one, including her, can recall it, POV hers. Magic is legal again, gardens grow in Grayhollow, and Sefa arrives to teach. August builds a life under a chosen name, mourning and free. The beat is bittersweet peace: she saved both realms and paid in identity, the theme made flesh.

chapters.title: Garden and Ember
chapters.summary: Epilogue, POV August. One year later, she tends a small garden behind her rebuilt shop, selling honest charms and keeping a blank-labeled bottle she never opens. A child asks about the empty label; August says it holds the most important memory she owns. The beat closes the arc — identity is not what you're given but what you choose to keep, and she chooses to keep going.
